title: Menopausal Symptoms, Mental Health and Psychosocial Functioning Among Postmenopausal Healthcare Workers: A Cross-Sectional Study
content: Objectives: To examine associations of menopausal symptoms, reproductive history, and socioeconomic and occupational factors with depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms and psychosocial functioning among postmenopausal healthcare workers. Methods: A single-centre cross-sectional study included 162 postmenopausal healthcare workers at a public general hospital in Greece. Data covered reproductive and menopausal characteristics, sociodemographic and occupational factors, mental health history and lifestyle. Outcomes were assessed using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) and Brief Inventory of Psychosocial Functioning (BIPF). Analyses included non-parametric tests, Spearman correlations and hierarchical linear regression. Results: Participants’ mean age was 55.35 years. The most frequently reported menopausal symptoms were mood changes (62.3%), reduced sexual desire (61.7%) and sleep changes (59.9%). In multivariable analyses, greater financial difficulty, previous mental health diagnosis, family history of mental illness and self-reported weight gain or fat redistribution were associated with higher BDI scores. Older age was associated with lower HAM-A scores (B = −0.495; 95% CI −0.823 to −0.167). Greater financial difficulty and holding a position of professional responsibility were associated with greater psychosocial impairment. Conclusions: Psychological symptoms and psychosocial impairment among postmenopausal healthcare workers were associated with socioeconomic circumstances, mental health history, perceived weight changes and professional responsibility. Assessment of women’s health needs after menopause should consider these concerns alongside menopausal symptoms. The cross-sectional design precludes conclusions about causality.
